lead: Exergy is the largest useful work a system or a stream can give as it comes to the dead state, exchanging heat only with the surroundings. Energy is always conserved, but exergy is not: every real process destroys some, and the amount destroyed is T₀ times the entropy generated. An exergy balance shows where a plant wastes its ability to do work, and the second law efficiency tells how close a device comes to the best possible device. Some syllabi call exergy "availability" and exergy destruction "irreversibility".
prereq: You need: Available and unavailable energy for the dead state, and the steady-flow energy equation and entropy generation from the first and second laws.

blocks.text: Take a closed system at a state (T, p) in surroundings at T₀ and p₀. As it comes to the dead state it can give work, but part of any expansion only pushes back the atmosphere. That part, p₀(V₂ − V₁), is not useful, so the useful work of a process is Wu = W − p₀(V₂ − V₁). The largest useful work, on a fully reversible path that exchanges heat only with the surroundings, is the exergy:
φ = (u − u₀) + p₀(v − v₀) − T₀(s − s₀)
blocks.where: φ is the specific exergy of the closed system in kJ/kg (add V²/2 and gz if it moves or is raised); u, v and s are the specific internal energy (kJ/kg), volume (m³/kg) and entropy (kJ/(kg·K)) at the state; subscript 0 marks the dead state; T₀ is in K and p₀ in kPa. The total exergy is Φ = mφ in kJ.

blocks.text: u − u₀ is the energy stored above the dead state; p₀(v − v₀) is the work exchanged with the atmosphere as the volume changes to v₀ (negative for a compressed gas); −T₀(s − s₀) is the heat that must pass to or from the surroundings to bring the entropy to s₀. The exergy is never negative and is zero only at the dead state.
Between two states the reversible useful work is the fall in exergy, W<sub>rev</sub> = Φ₁ − Φ₂, and the exergy destroyed is I = W<sub>rev</sub> − W<sub>u</sub>.

sections.h3: Flow exergy and the exergy balance

blocks.text: A stream crossing the boundary of a control volume also carries flow work pv, so its exergy uses enthalpy:
ψ = (h − h₀) − T₀(s − s₀) + V²/2 + gz
blocks.where: ψ is the flow exergy in kJ/kg; h is specific enthalpy in kJ/kg; V is velocity in m/s and z height in m (divide V²/2 and gz by 1000 to get kJ/kg). For most turbines and heat exchangers the last two terms are small and dropped.

blocks.text: For a steady device, per kg of flow, the exergy that comes in with heat and with the stream equals the work out, the exergy that leaves with the stream, and the exergy destroyed:
q<sub>k</sub> is heat received through a part of the boundary at temperature T<sub>k</sub>; w is the work out in kJ/kg; i is the exergy destroyed per kg.

blocks.where: This is the Gouy-Stodola theorem. s<sub>gen</sub> is the entropy generated per kg in kJ/(kg·K), found from an entropy balance; for an adiabatic steady device s<sub>gen</sub> = s₂ − s₁. In rate form, İ = T₀Ṡ<sub>gen</sub> in kW.

blocks.text: Exergy is destroyed by the same causes that generate entropy: friction, throttling, mixing, and heat transfer across a finite temperature difference. For an adiabatic turbine the balance becomes w = (ψ₁ − ψ₂) − T₀(s₂ − s₁): the work is the exergy drop less the exergy destroyed. Figure 4.2.1 draws this split for the first worked example.

First-law efficiency compares energy out with energy in. Second law efficiency compares the exergy recovered with the exergy supplied, so it measures how close a device is to the reversible one. A reversible device has η<sub>II</sub> = 1.
Both exergies are in the same units and measured from the same dead state.

blocks.text: Do not mix η<sub>II</sub> with the isentropic efficiency η<sub>is</sub> = (h₁ − h₂)/(h₁ − h₂s). The isentropic efficiency compares with an ideal turbine that ends at the same pressure; the second law efficiency compares with the whole exergy drop. In an adiabatic turbine whose expansion stays above T₀, the friction heat is still above T₀ and could do some work further down, so T₀s<sub>gen</sub> is smaller than the isentropic loss and η<sub>II</sub> comes out higher than η<sub>is</sub>.

An electric heater turns 1 kW of electricity into 1 kW of heat, a first-law efficiency of 100 %. Heat for a room at 295 K with the outside at T₀ = 278 K carries only 1 × (1 − 278/295) = 0.058 kW of exergy, so η<sub>II</sub> is about 5.8 %.

examples.question: Steam enters an adiabatic turbine with h₁ = 3200 kJ/kg and s₁ = 6.80 kJ/(kg·K) and leaves with h₂ = 2600 kJ/kg and s₂ = 7.00 kJ/(kg·K). The surroundings are at T₀ = 300 K. Neglect kinetic and potential energy. Find the work per kg, the exergy destroyed and the second law efficiency.
steps: Energy balance for the adiabatic turbine: w = h₁ − h₂ = 3200 − 2600 = 600 kJ/kg.
Entropy generated (adiabatic, steady): s<sub>gen</sub> = s₂ − s₁ = 7.00 − 6.80 = 0.20 kJ/(kg·K).
Exergy drop of the stream: ψ₁ − ψ₂ = (h₁ − h₂) − T₀(s₁ − s₂) = 600 − 300 × (6.80 − 7.00) = 600 + 60 = 660 kJ/kg. Check with the balance: w + i = 600 + 60 = 660 kJ/kg.
Second law efficiency: η<sub>II</sub> = w/(ψ₁ − ψ₂) = 600/660 = 0.909.
examples.answer: w = 600 kJ/kg, exergy destroyed = 60 kJ/kg, η<sub>II</sub> = 0.909 (90.9 %).

examples.question: 2 kg of air is held in a rigid tank at 500 kPa and 400 K. The surroundings are at 100 kPa and 300 K. Treat air as an ideal gas with c<sub>p</sub> = 1.005, c<sub>v</sub> = 0.718 and R = 0.287 kJ/(kg·K). Find the exergy of the air.
steps: Stored energy: u − u₀ = c<sub>v</sub>(T − T₀) = 0.718 × (400 − 300) = 71.8 kJ/kg.
examples.answer: The air holds Φ = 121.0 kJ of exergy (60.50 kJ/kg). The atmosphere term and the entropy term almost cancel here, so the exergy is not simply the stored internal energy of 143.6 kJ.

traps: Using ψ (with h) for a closed tank, or φ (with u) for a stream. A closed system uses u and p₀(v − v₀); a stream uses h.
Dropping the p₀(v − v₀) term. In the tank example it is −63.14 kJ/kg, larger than the final answer of 60.50 kJ/kg.
Taking the isentropic efficiency as the second law efficiency. They use different ideal references.
Writing s<sub>gen</sub> = s₁ − s₂ for an adiabatic device. Entropy generated is s₂ − s₁ ≥ 0, so exergy destroyed is never negative.

quiz.q: Write the flow exergy of a stream.
quiz.a: ψ = (h − h₀) − T₀(s − s₀) + V²/2 + gz, measured from the dead state.
The exergy destroyed equals T₀ times the entropy generated: I = T₀S<sub>gen</sub>.

quiz.q: An electric heater has a first-law efficiency of 100 %. Why is its second law efficiency low?
quiz.a: Electricity is pure exergy, but heat close to room temperature carries little exergy: η<sub>II</sub> = 1 − T₀/T<sub>room</sub>, about 5.8 % for a 295 K room with 278 K outside.

quiz.q: Steam in an adiabatic turbine: h₁ = 3000, h₂ = 2500 kJ/kg; s₁ = 6.50, s₂ = 6.80 kJ/(kg·K); T₀ = 300 K. Find w, i, ψ₁ − ψ₂ and η<sub>II</sub>.
quiz.a: w = 500 kJ/kg; s<sub>gen</sub> = 0.30 kJ/(kg·K); i = 90 kJ/kg; ψ₁ − ψ₂ = 500 + 90 = 590 kJ/kg; η<sub>II</sub> = 500/590 = 0.847.

quiz.q: In a heat exchanger the hot stream gives 200 kW of exergy and the cold stream gains 150 kW. Find η<sub>II</sub> and the exergy destroyed (no heat loss).
Steam is throttled adiabatically; its entropy rises from 6.0 to 6.3 kJ/(kg·K) and T₀ = 300 K. What happens to its exergy?
quiz.a: h is constant, so ψ₁ − ψ₂ = T₀(s₂ − s₁) = 300 × 0.3 = 90 kJ/kg, all destroyed, with no work. As a work-producing device the valve has η<sub>II</sub> = 0.

beyond: Exergy analysis is used in power-plant audits, heat-exchanger network design and building energy studies. Exergoeconomics puts a price on exergy destruction, so each rupee of lost work is charged to the equipment that causes it. Search next: exergy analysis of a power plant, exergoeconomics, pinch analysis.
